content: Ichthyosis refers to a group of genetic skin disorders that affect both humans and domestic animals. Individuals or animals with ichthyosis exhibit skin that is dry and scaly, often resembling the appearance of fish scales. The term ichthyosis originates from the Greek word ιχθύωσις, which translates to forming fish. This name reflects the characteristic scaly skin seen in affected individuals. Historically, ichthyosis was sometimes referred to as pseudo-leprosy due to its superficial resemblance to the skin changes seen in leprosy. While the term ichthyosis can refer to the broader group of conditions, it is also used specifically to describe ichthyosis vulgaris, one of the most common forms. Ichthyosis can be classified into congenital and acquired forms. The acquired form, known as ichthyosis acquisita, develops later in life, often secondary to other medical conditions. However, most types of ichthyosis are congenital, meaning they are present from birth. Examples of congenital ichthyosis include ichthyosis vulgaris, X-linked ichthyosis, lamellar ichthyosis, epidermolytic hyperkeratosis, harlequin ichthyosis, Netherton syndrome, and Sjögren-Larsson syndrome. The condition does not show any specific association with ethnicity, meaning it can affect individuals of any racial or ethnic background. In addition to humans, ichthyosis has been documented in certain breeds of domestic dogs. Breeds such as Golden Retrievers, American Bulldogs, Jack Russell Terriers, and Cairn Terriers are particularly prone to varying severities of ichthyosis. The clinical presentation of ichthyosis includes symptoms such as dry skin, scaly skin, and thickened skin. On physical examination, the hallmark findings are dry, scaly patches of skin. In cases of ichthyosis vulgaris, these findings are often more pronounced and can be confirmed through clinical observation. A definitive diagnosis may require a skin biopsy, which provides histological evidence of the condition. Treatment for ichthyosis primarily focuses on managing symptoms, as there is currently no cure. Topical therapies, including creams and emollient oils, are commonly used to hydrate the skin and reduce scaling. Retinoids, a class of medications derived from vitamin A, may be prescribed in certain cases to help regulate skin cell turnover. Ocular complications can occur in some forms of ichthyosis. For example, corneal and ocular surface diseases may develop, and vascularizing keratitis is a known complication, particularly in congenital keratitis-ichthyosis-deafness (KID) syndrome. It is important to note that isotretinoin therapy, while effective for some skin symptoms, may worsen vascularizing keratitis. Ectropion, a condition where the eyelids turn outward, can also occur in severe cases of ichthyosis. This can be managed surgically, but only after adequate hydration of the skin. At present, there are no known methods to prevent ichthyosis, and management remains focused on alleviating symptoms and improving the quality of life for affected individuals.
